The objectives of Apollo 9 and Apollo 10 differed primarily in their mission focus and location:

- Apollo 9's primary objective was an Earth-orbital engineering test of the first crewed lunar module (LM). It involved an overall checkout of the launch vehicle and spacecraft systems, crew, and procedures. The mission performed integrated flight tasks with the command module (CM), service module (SM), and LM in various docked and independent configurations. The LM was tested as a self-sufficient spacecraft and performed active rendezvous and docking maneuvers simulating those planned for Apollo 10.

- Apollo 10's mission encompassed all aspects of an actual crewed lunar landing except the landing itself. It was the first flight of a complete, crewed Apollo spacecraft to operate around the Moon. Objectives included an eight-hour lunar orbit of the separated LM, descent to about nine miles off the Moon’s surface, and ascent for rendezvous and docking with the command and service module in lunar orbit. Apollo 10 aimed to rehearse the lunar landing mission closely, gather data on lunar gravitational effects, refine tracking techniques, and check out LM programmed trajectories, radar, and lunar flight control systems.

In summary, Apollo 9 focused on testing the LM and spacecraft systems in Earth orbit, while Apollo 10 conducted a full lunar orbit mission simulating all aspects of a lunar landing except the actual touchdown.
